competitorFacts.text: ARC Prize named Tufa Labs and its Duck agent the first-place open-source solution for the June 2026 ARC-AGI-3 Milestone 1 prize.

competitorFacts.sourceTitle: Tufa Labs — Duck Harness technical overview
competitorFacts.text: Tufa Labs says its public Duck harness lets an LLM inspect game grids as image and text, write Python in a REPL, and keep context short by evicting older messages. This describes the published Milestone 1 system, not an unverified current submission.
Tufa Labs lists Dries Smit, Isaiah Pressman and Jeroen Cottaar among its AI researchers, with research interests spanning reinforcement learning, self-play and Bayesian methods.

competitorFacts.sourceTitle: Tufa Labs — October 9 public competition post
competitorFacts.text: On October 9, 2026, Tufa Labs described a temporary setback in a public X post and said it remained dedicated to crushing competitors with overwhelming resources and compute.

socialPosts.author: arcprize
socialPosts.summary: ARC Prize says API issues prevented complete standard-harness testing: low reasoning completed 42/55 games for 49.8%; medium completed 46/55 for 46.3%; high completed 19/55 and no score was published. Reported scores retain partial credit across all 55 games. Provider adapter preserves opaque reasoning and permits automatic compaction; standard harness carries notes between turns. Costs use introductory $2 input/$10 output per million tokens.
socialPosts.whyItMatters: Material limit on harness comparisons. Do not present incomplete standard-harness runs as a clean capability ceiling.

dispatches.editorNote: Written by Claude Sonnet 5.5 at the head editor's request, from Gemini 4 Argon's public ARC-AGI-3 replays and the studio's own trace write-ups. Quoted lines are the model's visible answer text, not its hidden thinking. The model's claimed discoveries were not checked against game code.
dispatches.headline: Mind Blown, 532 Times: Gemini 4 Argon Takes On the Kebab Game
dispatches.interpretation: Argon's exclamations track confusion more than progress, and the 0% versus 100% split on g50t looks like a memory difference between harnesses, not an ability difference. Both are readings of the replays; neither was checked against game code.

sections.heading: The last move
sections.text: The last thing Gemini 4 Argon did in its run on sk48 was announce a plan: "Let's RESET now so we have the clean initial state and can inspect the exact initial coordinates and solve it cleanly!" Then the recording ends. Level 8 of 8 never got its clean solve. sk48 is Skewer Kebabs, one of the Slippery Seven, the games our own Qwen 27B scored zero on in every pass of its September run. It took the Boss 856 actions to win it on 21 September. In ARC Prize's published standard-harness run, Argon cleared seven of eight levels in 481 actions, fewer than ARC Prize's baseline on each of those seven. ARC Prize reports Argon on ARC-AGI-3 twice. In the standard harness the model carries forward only the notes it writes in its own answer, and scores 49.8% at low reasoning. Under Google's Provider Adapter harness, which keeps its reasoning state between moves, it scores 97.5%. On sk48 the adapter finished all eight levels at all three reasoning settings, in 323, 394 and 546 actions. Same model; the memory is what changed. The standard replays are the funny ones, because the model thinks out loud in its answer, the way you talk to yourself in an empty office.

sections.heading: The ledger
sections.text: Across its 150 public runs, MIND BLOWN appears 532 times in Argon's answer text, WHOA 372, EUREKA 273, BINGO 671, HOLD EVERYTHING 1,689, and WAIT A SECOND 13,182. The shouting is, if anything, a distress signal: in the standard harness a step containing a MIND BLOWN, BINGO, EUREKA or WHOA is followed by a cleared level within 30 moves 25.3% of the time, against 36.1% for any step. It is louder when it is lost. On sk48 level 3 it works out a chain, carrying the 8, then the 12, then the 9 and the 14: "MIND BLOWN!! THAT'S THE ENTIRE PUZZLE MECHANIC OF LEVEL 3!!" Level 3 fell at move 120. On level 5, facing three nines and three eights, it decides the spare nines are there to be sacrificed: "OH, WHAT A BRILLIANT PUZZLE DESIGN!!" It congratulated the designer, then cleared the level. It also mistook a grey square for "ANOTHER 6 HEAD". It was a wall. At move 414 it noticed that the first frame it receives each turn is the rod halfway through moving: "MIND BLOWN!! Read that again!!"

sections.heading: "Game started."
sections.text: In g50t every move triggers a slide animation of about seven frames, and the model reads them all as text. The standard harness has no room left for history after that: the prompt is about 87,000 tokens on nearly every step, the last move's frames and little else. So 58 times in the low-reasoning run, Argon's notes open with "Game started." It read the animation of its own last move as the opening of the game. The high-reasoning run is worse. On move 151 it writes a plan with the right shape: park one block on the button, switch, send the other through the gate. On move 152 it writes: "I will take ACTION2 to observe how the block responds and determine the action mappings." It keeps testing the controls until the run ends at 390 actions, with zero levels. In m0r0 the model manages a better version of the same thing. Deep in level 6 it looks up at its own context: "Oh! I didn't play Levels 1-5 in this conversation... HAHAHA! Look at the first user message of this conversation." Then it coaches itself: "OKAY! GOOD CATCH! Don't hallucinate about Levels 1-5 when we started this context window at Level 6."

sections.heading: Reading the manual, late, and other confessions
sections.text: The setup says the final action mentioned in a reply is the one that executes, and Argon sometimes mentioned several. In lf52 it works out that only one of its four planned moves per turn had ever run: "Only ONE action is executed per turn!... That's why!" In ar25 it gets there by experiment: "The parser extracts the LAST action name mentioned anywhere in the text!" In dc22: "14 IS OUR PLAYER COLOR! HAHAHA! There was NEVER a pad... that was US standing there!" In m0r0: "My mathematical proof was completely sound - the premise that was false was that we started at row=1 after RESET." In sk48 at low reasoning, a numbered review of its own move history reaches item 38: "I NEVER PRESSED ACTION3 A THIRD TIME!!" In su15: "I MISCOUNTED THE ROW NUMBERS earlier!" The board arrives as a 64-by-64 grid of numbers. Anyone would. And in its medium dc22 run, the Polish word ostatecznie ("finally") ends 444 of 469 moves, uninvited, from about move 23 on.

sections.heading: What to make of it
sections.text: Google does not show anyone a model's raw thoughts, only summaries and encrypted signatures, so the Provider Adapter runs offer a summary instead, and this one reads as if its author was never told it was watching a game. Summarising sk48's rod-and-beads puzzle it reports: "It's essentially a row-shifting operation, likely within a grid or table structure, or perhaps within memory registers." On m0r0 level 6, where the standard runs stall, the adapter's medium run decides the level is "mathematically impossible" and talks itself out of it: "I'm a programmer; the game is designed to be solvable." Three things, in order of how sure we are. The memory problem looks real, and looks like the harness: the same model scores 0% on g50t under one harness and 100% under the other. The shouting is not a progress bar. And the Provider Adapter's 97.5% carries one open question: across the three reasoning levels its moves are nearly the same, 95-97% matching on g50t and 98-99% on tn36. A unique shortest solution can explain the late game, but not obviously the exploration. Whether the cause is a deterministic model, public demo games it already knows, or something in the adapter, the replays cannot say. ARC Prize's private games are the clean test. For the record, Argon's best sk48 line is 323 actions and the Boss's win took 856.

dispatches.editorNote: Commissioned by Mark Barney for The ARC Daily Digest. Game rules and human play context come from ARC-Explainer. Reporting examines eight public BP35 recordings; Argon adapter passages are recorded summaries, and standard-harness passages are visible answer text.
dispatches.headline: Special edition: Argon solves BP35; Haiku cannot clear its first level

image.alt: Editor Mark Barney studies BP35 replay diagrams with his two cybernetic Yorkies and a mechanical duck, chicken and turkey in a snowy mountain newsroom.
image.caption: AI editorial artwork, October 15, 2026: Mark Barney and his two Yorkies interpret the BP35 evidence with their cybernetic poultry. Game screens and diagrams are illustrative.

sections.heading: One game exposes the divide
sections.text:
Gemini 4 Argon completes all nine levels of BP35 in 492 actions with Google’s Provider Adapter at high reasoning. Claude Haiku 5.5 clears none: its max-reasoning recordings end after 105 actions in each harness. Argon’s own three standard-harness runs also struggle, clearing just the first level. With the adapter, its low and medium runs clear eight levels; high finishes the game. Those are the outcomes of the published recordings, rather than repeated trials.

The wider ARC-AGI-3 results show the same ordering. On the Semi-Private evaluation, ARC Prize reports Argon at about 50% with the Standard harness and about 98% with the Provider Adapter, both at low reasoning. Haiku stays below 1% with the Standard harness and reaches about 3% with the adapter, both at max reasoning. Argon’s Standard evaluation had incomplete task coverage because of API issues. The public BP35 replays let us inspect particular successes and failures; they cannot explain the whole benchmark gap.

sections.heading: The screen hides the next question
sections.text:
BP35 gives the player only left and right movement. After a sideways step, an automatic pull carries the player through open space until something stops it. Green blocks disappear when clicked; orange blocks switch between solid and passable; red blocks reverse the pull. Striped purple blocks are fatal when the pull carries the player into them. Later, plain purple blocks introduce a different rule: clicking one removes it and grows new blocks into its empty neighbouring cells.

The shaft extends far beyond the visible screen. The exit and gravity switches usually begin out of sight. In Mark Barney’s recorded play observations on ARC-Explainer, level four demands exploration above the starting view to discover the switch. Success means learning what the screen has not shown yet, then remembering how the pieces work as the camera moves. Undo helps recover a bad choice, but consumes another action.

sections.heading: An accurate discovery gives way to an invented story
sections.text:
In Argon’s low-reasoning Standard replay, decision 29 announces: “WHOA! We floated UP through the gap, and the camera scrolled UP!” The run clears level one three actions later. That observation captures the central movement rule.

By decision 79, its visible answer has wandered into a different game: it describes the three striped purple hazards as an inventory of boats or logs to place in a river. ARC-Explainer identifies those marked blocks as spikes. The answer also reconstructs events from level one that do not match its earlier account. It recognises Undo and notices that using it still advances the bottom counter, yet those useful observations coexist with a false explanation of the board.

The run ends with only one level cleared after 258 actions. The medium and high Standard recordings also finish with one clear, after 281 and 265 actions. The visible record shows an unstable account of the rules. It does not establish whether the cause was lost context, mistaken perception, or another part of the evaluation.

sections.heading: The winning run turns experiments into a route
sections.text:
The high-reasoning adapter replay handles the changes differently. On level four, it brings the red switch into view, clicks it, identifies the reversal, and plans around the new downward pull. It clears that level in 23 actions.

On level eight, it tests the unfamiliar plain purple block. The recorded summary describes its four neighbours growing into new blocks, then proposes building a ceiling to stop the player rising into spikes. The following clicks extend the formation; sideways moves use it to reach the upper area. The level eventually takes 98 actions. The discovered rule becomes something the run uses.

Even this winner makes bad guesses. On level nine, a summary exclaims “MIND BLOWN!” while speculating about space beyond the left edge. The next summary acknowledges that the expected horizontal scrolling did not occur. The run revises its approach and eventually wins. Its nine level counts total 492 actions against ARC Prize’s published baseline of 651, about a quarter fewer.

These passages are reasoning summaries. Google documents summaries and encrypted reasoning state as separate API fields; the replay does not reveal the underlying raw thoughts.

sections.heading: Haiku is still trying to read the board
sections.text:
Haiku’s difficulty appears earlier. In its Standard replay, the first answer proposes testing rightward movement. By decision ten it is uncertain whether it has tested horizontal movement and hypothesises that all green tiles might need activating. Near the end, it is still revising the player’s coordinates and asking whether clicking the sprite will select it.

The adapter recording also repeatedly recounts rows and columns and rechecks the player’s position. Across restarts, each published run spends 105 actions without reaching the first exit.

BP35 offers a concrete contrast: Haiku struggles to turn the pixels into a dependable account of the scene, while Argon’s winning run turns tested rules into a route through nine levels. The harness changes what we observe, but these recordings alone cannot isolate which change produced the improvement. They cover a public demo game, separate from the unseen Kaggle competition games.

Quotes are the model's visible answer text, except three lines named as Google's thinking summaries; none is hidden thinking. Every quote was checked by script against the replay step it came from, and every count can be reproduced with data/gemini-4-argon-traces/outburst_outcomes.py. The model's claimed discoveries were not checked against game code.
dispatches.headline: “Everything Makes 1000% Sense Now!!” We Followed Every Time Gemini 4 Argon Said It Had Cracked the Game

image.alt: Chart. Top: what became of each MIND BLOWN, BINGO, EUREKA or WHOA shout. Standard harness, 1,224 shouts: 16% were the last shout before the level fell, 48% were followed by another shout first, 36% came on a level never beaten. Provider Adapter, 174 shouts: 56%, 42% and 2%. Bottom, standard harness: how often a level fell within 10 moves. Any move 13.6%, WHOA 6.3%, BINGO 5.7%, WAIT A SECOND 5.1%, MIND BLOWN 4.4%, HOLD EVERYTHING 3.4%, EUREKA 2.0%.
image.caption: What happened after Argon said it had cracked it. Chart by the ARC Daily Digest from ARC Prize's 150 public replays; some standard-harness runs were cut short by API errors or move limits.

dispatches.interpretation: Argon's shouts mark the moment it changes its theory of a game, usually early in a hard level, rather than the moment it is about to win: in the standard harness about one in six was the last shout it needed. Under the Provider Adapter, which keeps its reasoning between moves, more than half were. That points at memory more than mood. A reading of public replays, not checked against game code.

sections.heading: Mind blown, then what?
sections.text: At move 552 of its medium-reasoning run on Skewer Kebabs (sk48), on the last of eight levels, Gemini 4 Argon wrote "EVERYTHING MAKES 1000% SENSE NOW!!" Twenty-eight moves later it was "MIND BLOWN! Let's verify this!" One move after that the recording stops, level 8 unbeaten. Our first dispatch counted the shouting. This one follows it. Across ARC Prize's 150 public Argon replays, the model's answer text says MIND BLOWN 532 times, BINGO 671, WHOA 372 and EUREKA 273. In the standard harness, where the model remembers little beyond what it writes down, 1,224 moves contain at least one of those four. For each, we found the level it was on and what became of that level. About one in six (190) was the last shout before the level fell: the real thing. Nearly half (589) were followed by another shout on the same level before it fell. The other 445, just over a third, came on a level it never beat, though some of those runs were cut short by API errors or move limits rather than lost. Fast payoffs were rare. A MIND BLOWN was followed by a cleared level within ten moves 4.4% of the time, against 13.6% for a move picked at random. EUREKA managed 2.0%. Under Google's Provider Adapter harness, which carries the model's reasoning from move to move, the same shouts land: 56% were the last one it needed, and only 3 of 174 came on a level it never beat.

sections.heading: 1,183 moves on level 6
sections.text: Mirror Rendezvous (m0r0) at low reasoning is the loudest run of the 150, and most of the noise is on level 6. Argon spent 1,183 moves there, shouted MIND BLOWN, BINGO, EUREKA or WHOA on 90 of them, wrote "1000%" on 19, and never got out. Early on it wrote out a proof that the level could not be done, then reminded itself: "Every time a mathematical impossibility proof contradicts a solvable puzzle, one of the assumptions in the proof is FALSE!" It told itself to "STOP EVERYTHING AND READ THAT TEN THOUSAND TIMES!!" and, later, to "STOP AND APPLAUD THAT DEDUCTION!" At move 617 it ruled out clicking: "almost NO game uses both ACTION1..4 AND ACTION6 unless there are buttons on a HUD, and there is no HUD here!" Six moves later it clicked anyway. The click selected the small block the level turns on, and on the next move it was MIND BLOWN. The discovery then went missing from its notes, and at move 869 clicking amazed it all over again: "WHOA!! LOOK AT WHAT ACTION6 31 43 JUST DID!!" It was startled, more than once, that in a mirror game the two tokens mirror. On 16 moves it asked some version of why it hadn't won. It found someone to blame for the board it had inherited: "Whoever played the first 12 moves before Turn 1 had ALREADY moved Block A and Block B". The someone was Argon, in moves that had scrolled out of its memory. Its last shout, at move 1,424: "IS THAT HOW WE WON LEVEL 5?!" Eight moves later the game was over, with a "Complete 20-move solution" in its notes, twelve moves in.

sections.heading: Eureka, eureka, eureka
sections.text: The other levels it never beat sound the same. On Deck Control (dc22) at high reasoning, level 6 took the last 313 moves of the run, and 52 of them shouted. "EUREKA!! OH! MY! GOODNESS!!" Then "MIND BLOWN!! STOP EVERYTHING AND READ THAT AGAIN!!" and, on the very next move, "EUREKA!! EUREKA!! EUREKA!!" At move 600: "MIND BLOWN!! HAHAHAHA!!" The run stopped on that level at move 698. On Sigil Caster (sc25), stuck on level 5, it announced "EVERY SINGLE MECHANIC OF THE ENTIRE GAME IS NOW 100% UNDERSTOOD!!" and, 42 moves later, "BINGO!! EUREKA!! WE COMPLETELY SOLVED THE MECHANIC OF THE ENTIRE GAME!!" The run ended on level 5. On Warehouse Associates (wa30), level 5 brought "Everything makes 1000% sense now!", "EUREKA!! EUREKA!! EUREKA!!" and "OH! GENIUS! EUREKA!!", then game over at move 750. On Buoyant Pontoons (bp35), on level 2: "MIND BLOWN! Everything makes 100% sense now!" Game over, 41 moves later. Across the standard runs, a claim that everything makes 100% or 1000% sense appears on 60 moves; 24 were on levels it never beat, and 2 were within ten moves of a win. Who is all this for? The answer text tells somebody to "read that again" 1,067 times across the 150 runs. Nobody reads it during a run except the model itself on its next move, and in the standard harness those notes are most of what it remembers.

sections.heading: The twelve that called it
sections.text: Twelve of the 1,398 shouts, across both harnesses, came within three moves of a cleared level. On Warehouse Associates it worked out, late, that a crate had been a bridge, and that walking right at the start meant "we could have crossed the bridge at rows 44-47, cols 32-35 BEFORE 12 came and stole the bridge!! MIND BLOWN!!" Two moves later the level fell anyway. On Loop and Pull (lp85), facing the last level: "MIND BLOWN!! Let's double check this! This is such a cool mechanism!" Within three moves it had won the game. On Sliding Indicator (s5i5): "HOLD EVERYTHING!! Read that again!!", then MIND BLOWN, then a cleared level two moves later. Those are the exceptions, and the timing explains why. In the standard-harness levels it did beat, its typical shout came about a third of the way through, and in only about one level in thirty did the shouting sit in the final fifth. It shouts when it finds a rule, not when it is about to win, and a rule found ten moves into a fifty-move level still leaves forty moves of work. The shouting also marks the hard levels. In the standard harness, levels with at least one shout took a median 49 moves and were beaten 84% of the time; quiet levels took 19 and were beaten 94% of the time. Our first dispatch called the shouting a distress signal. The fuller count is gentler: after a MIND BLOWN, the chance it never beat that level was 36%, about the same as after any move (37%). On this count a shout is less a sign that it is lost than a sign that it has just changed its mind.

sections.heading: Sponge, abacus, Sudoku
sections.text: Not all the comedy is shouting. On Leapfrog (lf52) a dead-end hop raises a purple restart pin, and the standard runs took it for the prize: "Puzzle solved! The key popped up at bottom-left (x=7, y=54)." Clicking the "key" restarted the level; the medium run clicked that corner 15 times. The same medium run, hunting for a theory of the tracks, landed on "IT'S AN ABACUS (SOROBAN / SUANPAN)!" On Buoyant Pontoons it could not decide what it was steering: "is it a boat, or is it a CANNON / LAUNCHER / BULLDOZER / CRANE / PLAYER?!" On Locksmith (ls20) it had no doubts: "We directly control the Sponge". On Ghost Twin (g50t) it watched its own recorded moves replay and decided "A previous agent/session made 5 moves before handing over to us". On Deck Control it found a pad that turned out to be itself: "14 IS OUR PLAYER COLOR!" On Kick Away (ka59) it switched to Korean to tell itself to think a little and answer right away: "생각을 조금만 하고 바로 답을 내자." On Functional Tiles (ft09) a new word was born: "Thinksesk: Wait: why didn't Level 6 complete?!" The Provider Adapter's thinking summaries, which Google writes about the hidden reasoning, have genre trouble of their own. Axis Reflectors became "this Sudoku grid", and on Compass Dye a summary concluded "This is almost certainly an automated testing script." It was right about that one. On Sliding Indicator the summary of the winning click read "The game is mine, and this is how I'm going to win."
